title: Looking on him, loved him (Mark 10:17–31)
hookLine: the rich young man asks, Jesus loves him, and he goes away sad

lines: A MAN RUNS UP AND KNEELS.
cards: Jesus is setting out on the road again when a man comes running up and drops to his knees in the dust. Running. Kneeling.
He really wants an answer: good master, what must I do to receive eternal life? He's done everything right, kept the commandments since he was a boy. He's not a villain in this story.
He's the kind of person any parish would love to have. What happens next is sad, and it's also tender.

teach.h: JESUS LOOKED AT HIM AND LOVED HIM.
teach.b: First, the look. Jesus lists the commandments, and the man says he's kept them all from his youth. Then Mark adds, in the Douay-Rheims: "And Jesus looking on him, loved him."
Before the hard part, before any test. Matthew and Luke tell this story too, and neither keeps that line. Mark does.

teach.h: ONE THING IS WANTING: COME, FOLLOW.
teach.b: "One thing is wanting unto thee: go, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." The same invitation the fishermen got.
In Mark's order, the love comes first, then the hard words. Third, the face.
His face fell, and he went away sorrowful, "for he had great possessions." Not angry. Sad.

He wanted it, and he couldn't let go. Mark never says whether he came back; the sources are silent. And only Matthew calls him young, only Luke a ruler: the rich young ruler is three Gospels folded together.
Fourth, the camel. It's easier, Jesus says, for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom. The stunned disciples ask: then who can be saved?

teach.h: IMPOSSIBLE WITH MEN, NOT WITH GOD.
teach.b: He looks at them too: "With men it is impossible; but not with God."

teach.h: AND JESUS LOOKING ON HIM, LOVED HIM.
teach.b: Athanasius tells how a young Egyptian named Anthony heard Jesus's words to a rich man read aloud in church, gave his land away, and went into the desert.
Catholic teaching treats selling everything as a call some receive, not a rule for all. But in Mark, the look of love comes before any of it.

how: Catholic religious brothers and sisters take a vow of poverty, following this invitation literally, while lay Catholics are taught to practice detachment and generosity, often through almsgiving, especially in Lent.

o: the easy fondness of close friends and family
romantic love, the kind between partners
a self-giving love that wants another's good

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: loved him, before the hard part
heard it read and gave his land away

s: all three Gospels say Jesus loved him
only Mark keeps "looking on him, loved him."
Mark calls him a rich young ruler
only Matthew says young and only Luke says ruler; the popular name folds all three together.
the man goes away sad, not angry
he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.

games.q: you're the rich man. Jesus looks at you with love and says: sell what you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me. what do you do?
o: argue that the commandments are enough.
games.why: he went away sorrowful, "for he had great possessions." Mark never says whether he came back.

practice: Imagine being looked at the way the man was: not inspected, loved, and stay in that a while.

Then think of one thing you own and hold a little too tightly, not everything, just one, a jacket, a book, a gadget, a sum of money, and picture who might need it. If you pray, you can ask for open hands.

wordCard.voice: Agape. The Greek word for love Mark uses here: Jesus looked at the rich man, and loved him, before asking anything hard. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he loved him, from agapē. only Mark keeps it.

carryVoice: Your line: he loved him first. Even the one who walked away. See you tomorrow.
